newsitem.title: UK: Nickel physical market seen firming, scrap tighter.
newsitem.headline: Nickel physical market seen firming, scrap tighter.

text.p: Supply of nickel scrap is tightening as stainless steel mills operate at full capacity, and physical nickel premiums are expected to soon feel the heat, traders said.
The early flooding of the Russian port of Dudinka has already reduced availability of Russian material, they added.
"There is no question that if the mills continue to go at full speed they will have to reduce their scrap ratio," one said.
One mill is now only able to cover 60 percent of its requirements with scrap, compared to the 80 percent level that most mills prefer, he added.
"We've been selling full plate to a mill in Pittsburgh for the first time in a long while," he said.
Another physical trader said that although scrap supply was thinner, the market was not as tight as expected. "Scrap is not as abundant as before, but there's not a shortage either," he said.
"All logic says they should be running out of scrap...Maybe there's a new source of scrap that we don't know about," he added.
Traders said the premium of plating metal, cif Rotterdam, has remained steady at $280/$300 per tonne over LME cash, although one industry source put it lower at $220/$280.
The discount for Russian uncut metal in Rotterdam was expected to shrink now that shipments out of Dudinka port, Norilsk's main export outlet, have been halted due to seasonal flooding.
Several traders said the discount was stable at $50/$80 under LME cash, but one said it had already tightened to $40/$50.
The flooding at Dudinka came earlier than expected and two ships planning to take 8,000 tonnes of metal were not able to load, a trader said.
"People had been expecting the flooding around May 9-12, but it happened early on May 2," he said.
The market was also watching the labour contract expiry at the end of May at Inco Ltd's Ontario division, which produces 240 million lb of nickel and 237 million lb of copper per year.

The physical market was not behind the recent spike in three month prices, but steady consumer interest gave the market a firm underpinning over the past several weeks as futures explored the downside, traders said.
